title: Linux Fundamentals
summary: Linux is the operating system that runs virtually all production infrastructure. Understanding its filesystem layout, permissions model, process management, and package system is the foundation everything else in DevOps builds on.

sections.title: The Linux filesystem hierarchy
sections.body:
Linux follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). Every file lives under `/` (root). Knowing what lives where stops you from getting lost.

```
/
├── bin/     → essential user binaries (ls, cp, bash)
├── sbin/    → system binaries (reboot, fdisk)
├── etc/     → configuration files — the most important directory for ops
├── var/     → variable data: logs (/var/log), spool, cache
├── home/    → user home directories (/home/esteban)
├── root/    → root user's home
├── tmp/     → temporary files, cleared on reboot
├── usr/     → read-only user data; usr/bin, usr/local/bin for installed programs
├── opt/     → optional software packages (self-contained installations)
├── proc/    → virtual filesystem: running kernel and process info
├── sys/     → virtual filesystem: device and kernel info
├── dev/     → device files (disks, terminals, /dev/null, /dev/random)
├── lib/     → shared libraries for /bin and /sbin
└── mnt/     → temporary mount points
```

The ones you'll touch most in DevOps:

```bash
# Configuration — edit with care
ls /etc/apt/             # apt config (nginx not installed in sandbox)
ls /etc/systemd/system/  # systemd service files
cat /etc/hosts           # local hostname resolution
cat /etc/resolv.conf     # DNS resolver config

# Logs — your first stop when something breaks
tail /var/log/dpkg.log 2>/dev/null | head -5  # package install log
# journalctl requires systemd — not available in containers (use kubectl logs instead)

# Kernel and hardware info via /proc
cat /proc/cpuinfo     # CPU details
cat /proc/meminfo     # memory details
cat /proc/version     # kernel version
```

sections.title: Users, groups, and permissions
sections.body:
Linux permissions determine who can read, write, or execute a file. Getting these wrong is a common cause of both broken deployments and security incidents.

```bash
# ls -l output format:
# -rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devs 4096 Jan 1 10:00 script.sh
#  ^^^^^^^^^
#  |└──┬──┘└──┬──┘└──┬──┘
#  |   │      │      └── other: r-- (read only)
#  |   │      └──────── group: r-x (read + execute)
#  |   └─────────────── owner: rwx (read + write + execute)
#  └─────────────────── file type (- file, d dir, l symlink)

# Each permission set: r=4, w=2, x=1
# rwxr-xr-- = 7 5 4 = 754

# chmod — change permissions
chmod 755 /workspace/check_images.py   # rwxr-xr-x  (owner: all, group: r+x, other: r+x)
chmod 644 /workspace/config.yaml       # rw-r--r--  (owner: r+w, group: r, other: r)
chmod -R 755 /workspace               # recursive

# chown — change owner
chown root /workspace/config.yaml  # running as root already

# Users and groups
id                    # show current user, uid, gid, groups
whoami                # just the username
groups                # show groups you belong to

# sudo — run as root
apt update -qq 2>/dev/null | tail -1

# Special permissions
# setuid (4xxx): run as file owner, not caller — used by /usr/bin/passwd
# setgid (2xxx): run as file group
# sticky bit (1xxx): only owner can delete — used on /tmp
ls -la /tmp | head -3  # drwxrwxrwt ← t = sticky bit
```

Key principle: **least privilege**. Application processes should run as a dedicated non-root user with only the permissions they need.

sections.title: Process management
sections.body:
Every running program is a process with a PID (process ID). DevOps work constantly involves starting, stopping, and inspecting processes.

```bash
# View processes
ps aux                   # all processes, BSD style
ps aux | grep nginx      # find nginx processes
ps -ef --forest          # tree view showing parent/child

# top / htop — interactive process viewer
top                  # CPU, memory, load average, per-process view
# In top: press M (sort by memory), P (sort by CPU), k (kill), q (quit)
# htop is the friendlier version — try: htop

# Key process info
# PID   # process ID — used to signal/kill
# PPID  # parent PID
# UID   # user running the process
# CPU%  # CPU usage
# MEM%  # memory usage
# STAT  # state: R(running), S(sleeping), Z(zombie), D(disk wait)

# Signals
kill -0 $$ 2>/dev/null && echo "process $$ exists"  # -0 checks existence without killing
kill -1 1234    # SIGHUP: reload config (used by nginx, sshd)
pkill -0 nginx 2>/dev/null && echo nginx running || echo nginx not running
pkill -f pattern # kill processes matching a pattern

# Background and foreground
sleep 5 &           # run in background
jobs                # list background jobs
# fg/bg require interactive shell (job control); fg 1 / bg 1
nohup sleep 3 &    # keep running after logout

# systemd — the modern way to manage services
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl status nginx        # show status
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl start nginx         # start service
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl stop nginx          # stop service
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl restart nginx       # restart (stop + start)
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl reload nginx        # reload config without restart
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl enable nginx        # start automatically at boot
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl disable nginx       # remove autostart
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running  # list running services
```

sections.title: Package management & software installation
sections.body:
Different Linux distributions use different package managers. Debian/Ubuntu use `apt`, RHEL/CentOS use `yum`/`dnf`, Alpine uses `apk`.

```bash norun
# ── Debian / Ubuntu (apt) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Update package list (always do this first)
apt update

# Install a package
apt install -y nginx curl git

# Remove a package
apt remove nginx
apt purge nginx      # also removes config files

# Search for a package
apt search nginx

# Show package info
apt show nginx

# Upgrade all installed packages
apt upgrade -y

# ── RHEL / CentOS / Rocky (yum / dnf) ─────────────────────────────────────
yum install -y nginx
dnf install -y nginx   # newer RHEL/CentOS 8+

# ── Alpine (used in Docker images) ────────────────────────────────────────
apk add nginx curl git
apk del nginx

# ── Installing from binary / tarball ──────────────────────────────────────
# Many DevOps tools aren't in package managers
# Pattern: download, verify, install to /usr/local/bin
curl -LO https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.29.4/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl
chmod +x kubectl
mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/

# Pattern: extract tarball
tar -xzf tool-v1.0.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv tool /usr/local/bin/

# Check what's installed
which kubectl       # find the binary
kubectl version     # confirm it works
dpkg -l | grep nginx  # list installed debian packages
rpm -qa | grep nginx  # list installed rpm packages
```

In Docker containers, the image typically uses `apt` or `apk`. In the sandbox backend container (Debian-based), `apt` is available but most tools are pre-installed.

sections.title: Exercise: explore the sandbox Linux environment
sections.body:
Use the terminal to answer the following questions about the sandbox environment:

```bash
# 1. What Linux distribution and kernel version is running?
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r

# 2. What user are you running as? What groups?
id

# 3. How much memory is available? How much disk?
free -h
df -h /

# 4. What processes are using the most CPU right now?
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10

# 5. Find all files in /workspace
find /workspace -type f
ls -la /workspace

# 6. Inspect the /etc directory — what config files exist?
ls /etc | head -20

# 7. Check which tools are installed and where they live
which kubectl helm argocd python3 jq

# 8. Look at the running services (systemd is not used here — Docker)
# Instead, see what processes are running:
ps aux | grep -v grep

# 9. Find the kubeconfig file and examine it (without printing sensitive data)
ls -la /tmp/k3s.yaml
cat /tmp/k3s.yaml | grep -v 'certificate\|key'

# 10. Check disk usage of the /data directory
du -sh /data/*
```

**Bonus:** The `/proc` filesystem is live kernel data. Try:

```bash
cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '    # what is PID 1 running?
ls /proc/ | grep '^[0-9]' | wc -l   # how many processes exist?
cat /proc/meminfo | grep MemTotal    # total memory in kB
```
